content:
Human judgement, verification, and transparency remain critical AI-era advantages

After all the doom and gloom surrounding AI-triggered job losses, here's some comforting news on a Monday morning. The latest evidence on AI and Indian work isn't suggesting that humans are becoming obsolete. On the contrary, it seems like as more people use AI, the ones who truly excel at it are increasingly deciding what AI should and shouldn't be trusted with.

There are two interesting signals that point to this trend. Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index reports that 32% of Indian AI users are now "Frontier Professionals," which is just a fancy term for people who are deploying agentic workflows with multi-step automation, thereby reshaping existing work patterns. The global average for this is 16%, which tells you something about the general readiness and attitude towards embracing AI at Indian workplaces.

On the other end of the AI continuum is Indeed's inaugural Hiring Confidence Index, which gives India just 58 out of 100 for confidence in the hiring process. When you read Microsoft's report in tandem with Indeed's, it makes for a more nuanced story than merely screaming "AI is taking jobs."

AI isn't about intelligent chatbots anymore

According to Microsoft's report, as much as 78% of Indian AI users are using AI in ways which wasn't possible a year ago, which allows them to work in novel ways, of course - this number jumps to 85% among Frontier Professionals. This is an interesting insight which goes beyond the age-old AI conversation around productivity gains inside a chat window - summarising emails, rewriting paragraphs, formatting spreadsheets, and more.

The Indian workforce is fast embracing agentic orchestration for reimagining AI workflows, as they move beyond AI pilots to broad scale agentic integration and deployment. About 34% of Indian organisations already have functional agent workflows running, according to Microsoft, versus 26% globally.

Also read: Is AI replacing jobs or creating them? Here is what LinkedIn data says

But even here, I feel, the most interesting data point is related to how humans are using AI in the workplace. Quality control of AI output is becoming more important for 63% of Indian respondents, while 59% pick critical thinking as the most important consideration. As many as 87% of human respondents claim they are responsible for thinking - even if it's assisted by AI - and treat AI output as a suggestion, not the end goal, according to Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index.

AI's role in hiring is a mixed bag

Before entering the workplace, Indeed's findings point to a similar shift in job seekers and their expectations. According to Indeed, as many as 54% of Indian jobseekers want skills assessments to be more important than just reading a CV. Especially, Gen Z are increasingly demanding this more than any other demographic - where 63% expressed support for tests and task-based assessments.

title: AI impact on Indian workplaces: Humans are getting more important
author: Digit

For first-time workers entering an AI-disrupted workplace, the safest career choice may be not choosing a fixed path.

Curiosity, adaptability and human skills could matter more than early specialisation, said True Group chief executive Sigve Brekke, whose unconventional journey illustrates that message.

Raised on a small mountain farm in Norway, he once expected to become a farmer. Instead, his first job was teaching a sixth-grade class at 19. He later moved through farming, advertising and politics, becoming Norway's deputy minister of defence at 30.

After earning a master's degree at Harvard University, his curiosity about Asia steered him towards telecoms. Despite having no experience, he joined Telenor and was sent to explore opportunities in Asia, eventually becoming chief executive of Total Access Communication and later Telenor's global chief executive.

Looking back, Mr Brekke said his career was largely unplanned.

His advice to young people is to focus on doing their current job well, remain curious and avoid specialising too soon.

"Try to learn as much as possible about as much as possible because the world and business continue to get more complex," Mr Brekke said in a panel discussion moderated by Spring News.

"Don't specialise too early. Move around, try new things."

Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said a perceived mismatch between what students study and where they eventually work is not necessarily a failure.

"Learning should not be limited by age. A master's degree may not be enough for lifelong learning," he said. "I encourage continued training."

Universities should evolve beyond lecture halls into "incubators", allowing students to gain real-world experience, build networks and explore entrepreneurship, said Mr Yodchanan.

Young Thais should also strengthen practical skills in communication, presentation, entrepreneurship and financial literacy, he said.

His own career changed sharply at 46, when he moved from academia into politics.

"I changed my job at 46 from professor to politician, and I might lose my job at any time," said Mr Yodchanan. "But I'm not afraid. What we gain is experience, so we can start again with those skills."

HOURGLASS WORKFORCE

Mr Brekke said he expects artificial intelligence (AI) to reshape companies into an "hourglass" structure: senior leaders at the top for critical thinking and decision-making, AI-native young talent at the bottom and a thinner middle as routine management tasks are automated.

Career paths could split accordingly. Management positions may become harder to secure as middle layers shrink, while specialist careers built around deep expertise expand.

He suggested companies create shadow junior management teams to inject younger AI-native perspectives into senior decision-making. Leaders must understand AI well enough to identify new business models, products and automated processes. Those who fail to adapt, warned Mr Brekke
title: Rethinking work in the AI era
author: Bangkok Post

As a dominatrix drag queen struts through a crowd with her eyes set on tackling corporate greed, she uses brute force to throw aside actors portraying the tech giants locals blame for rising power prices.

It's an unusual display of theatrics, aimed at firing up fed-up residents of North Carolina, on the east coast of the United States, who say data centres are driving up their power bills, before they are even built.

On the front steps of a Durham courthouse in June, hundreds of community members lined up to voice their concerns about a proposed 18 per cent rise in their electricity bills, which they blamed on new infrastructure needed for data centres.

A chorus, led by local activists The Raging Grannies, led the group in song.

It is a show of support against what the protesters say is corporate greed.

But when it comes to data centres in the US, it is not just the environment and human health locals were concerned about.

The opposition to data centres at the rally was also ideological, with protesters against the storing of surveillance material, and artificial intelligence taking jobs.

They are all arguments about an industry which has grown from about 3,000 data centres in 2021 to about 4,000 in 2026, according to the World Resources Institute.

Noise, diesel concerns

The Drag Down Our Electric Bills Rally attracted hundreds of peaceful protesters, who said big tech was responsible for their growing bills.

Duke Energy, the privately owned power company that generates and supplies electricity to consumers, applied to the North Carolina utilities commissioner to increase prices by 18 per cent.

Prior to a repeal of tax incentives in July, data centre companies in North Carolina paid no tax on their electricity usage as a drawcard to attract investment.

It is now home to about 90 data centres and successfully brought companies Apple, Meta and Google south of Virginia, the data centre capital.

The actual power price rises for North Carolina are still under negotiation and are yet to be signed off by the utilities commission.

Local science teacher Carl Hintz was part of the protest.

"This electric company is making the argument they need to produce even more electricity to be able to power these data centres," he said.

"Even though these data centres haven't been built yet, it's already impacting people with higher electricity bills because of the anticipation that it might be built."

Lynne Taylor lives two hours away in Charlotte, where there are about 35 data centres, according to the international Data Center Map.

She said she was concerned about regional data centres taking up agricultural land alongside noise, health and environmental impacts.

She was also opposed to AI replacing jobs.

"What we have learned in America is that [you're] more likely to get kicked by a kangaroo than see any real economic gain for citizens," Mrs Taylor said.

"The developers of data centres promise many jobs for humans, but frankly, the majority
title: Americans urge caution as Australia braces for data centre boom
author: Australian Broadcasting Corporation

Businesses across Wales are being invited to harness the next generation of AI and cyber talent through Tech Talent Cymru, a new graduate placement programme supported by funding from Innovate UK, part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

Participating SMEs will receive more than £3,000 towards salary costs during the placement, helping them access specialist skills while giving graduates a meaningful first step into the technology sector.

Delivered by Darogan, Tech Talent Cymru connects Welsh SMEs with STEM graduates who have developed an understanding of artificial intelligence and cyber security through their university degrees. Graduates will also receive dedicated training before joining a business, alongside mentoring throughout the programme, enabling them to work on real projects from day one while continuing to receive support during their placement.

For employers, the programme offers an affordable way to bring new digital capability into the business and support digital transformation projects that many SMEs simply do not have the time or resources to tackle.

Owain James, founder of Darogan, said:

"There is a lot of conversation about AI replacing jobs, particularly for young people entering the workplace. Those concerns are real, but there is another crucial conversation to be had: AI is also creating a need for new skills. Businesses need people who understand these technologies and, more importantly, know how to apply them in practical ways.

"Tech Talent Cymru is about creating those opportunities. Graduates gain meaningful experience, while Welsh businesses gain fresh skills, new ideas and dedicated capacity to explore AI and strengthen cyber resilience.

"This is an investment in the future of both our businesses and our young people."

Tech Talent Cymru will be officially launched at GradCon Cymru, Darogan's annual graduate careers event, taking place at DEPOT Cardiff on 8 and 9 September. Businesses are encouraged to register their interest early so they can be matched with graduate talent best suited to their business needs.

For Welsh businesses, Tech Talent Cymru offers a practical way to access emerging AI and cyber skills without the cost of hiring specialist consultants or building new teams from scratch. For graduates, it provides the opportunity to build meaningful careers by helping businesses solve real-world challenges. By bringing the two together, the programme aims to strengthen Welsh businesses while helping talented graduates build their careers in Wales.

For more information or to register your interest in hosting a graduate, visit www.darogan.wales/techtalentcymru.
title: New Programme to Bring AI and Cyber Graduate Talent into Welsh SMEs
author: Business News Wales

The big picture: The reductions come amid a fervent conversation over the role of AI in replacing jobs, but Uber didn't cite AI as a catalyst for the cuts.

Driving the news: Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in an internal memo that the company is "removing layers, simplifying team structures, refining our global location strategy, and focusing our people and investments against the biggest opportunities ahead of us."

* The company had about 36,600 employees globally as of June 30, according to a public filing.

Zoom in: Many of the cuts are aimed at reducing middle management, including "micro-teams" where managers have only one to two people reporting to them.

* The company also reduced the number of employees who are at least seven layers down from the CEO by 20%.

* And Uber is ending remote work for most employees -- "going forward, only ~1% of employees will be remote," Khosrowshahi said.

"The changes we're making today are designed to do two things: make Uber simpler and faster, and create more capacity to invest in our future," Khosrowshahi said in the memo.

* "A leaner organization will mean clearer ownership, faster decisions, and more time spent building rather than coordinating. It will also generate savings that we intend to reinvest in growth, innovation, and the capabilities that will matter most over the coming years."

* He said the cuts were not reflective of the status of the business, which "is performing so well" and adding new products.

As Uber grew in recent years, it added "more layers, more coordination, more fragmented ownership, and in some cases structures that made sense when businesses were smaller but no longer serve us well at our current scale," Khosrowshahi said.

The impact: Uber shares were up just over 1% in early trading Wednesday.
title: Uber to cut 10% of workforce
author: Axios

Artificial intelligence could help the Eastern Cape overcome one of its biggest tourism challenges -- getting more international visitors to discover the province and stay longer.

Tourism industry leaders and government officials used the provincial launch of Tourism Month 2026 at Asante Estate outside KuGompo City on Tuesday to argue that better use of AI and digital technology could help close the gap between the Eastern Cape's natural attractions and its relatively small share of international tourists.

The province boasts seven of SA's nine biomes, with several converging around Port Alfred, while conservation land has expanded from virtually nothing a century ago to more than 450,000ha.

Yet the Eastern Cape attracts only about 3% to 4% of international visitors to SA, while about 76% head to either Cape Town or the Kruger National Park.

Chris Roberts, who operates five-star properties Oceana and Prana Lodge and heads the Wild Eastern Cape initiative, said technology offered the province an opportunity to improve its visibility internationally.

"From a tourism point of view, I'd put the impact of AI in these simple terms -- the travel agent used to be a person, then it was Google and the OTAs, now increasingly it is a machine that reads your websites and decides whether it wants to mention you at all," Roberts said.

"And this is where we need to leverage as a province.

"It's the easiest way for us to get our story out to the world, to grow visitor numbers and, in turn, to grow jobs and investment."

Roberts said optimising his properties' websites so that AI systems could better read and interpret their content had transformed web traffic within six months.

AI-generated referrals now accounted for more than 10% of monthly website visitors -- about 1,000 potential guests per property -- and produced the properties' highest conversion rate, he said.

He warned that tourism businesses which failed to structure their online content so that large language models could understand it risked being overlooked or inaccurately represented by AI systems.

Roberts also called for tourism operators across the province to collaborate on linked itineraries aimed at extending average stays from two or three nights to a week.

While acknowledging concerns about AI replacing jobs, he said tourism remained dependent on human interaction and that automation could instead free staff from repetitive administrative work.

"A reservationist who spends most of her day typing the same email over and over is not doing the thing she is actually good at," Roberts said.

"Take that work away, and you don't have a redundancy, you have someone who can spend her day selling the province, building itineraries, and turning a three-night booking into a seven-night one."

Economic development, environmental affairs and tourism MEC Nonkqubela Pieters said greater digital access also had to translate into economic opportunities for rural and coastal communities.

"For many
title: Intelligent use of AI can change Eastern Cape's tourism landscape

Smartphones, tablets, and smart assistants are all AI-integrated.

AI powers everything -- from search engines and social media algorithms to medical diagnostics and virtual assistants. But behind the polished surface lies an unsettling truth: prolonged exposure to AI-driven systems may be impacting our physical and mental health.

Here's how.

1. Mental Health Toll from Social Media Algorithms

AI is at the heart of modern social platforms. It decides what you see, what goes viral, and what gets buried. Algorithms are designed to keep users hooked -- leading to compulsive scrolling, addiction, and unhealthy comparison.

A study by the University of Pennsylvania found that limiting social media use to 30 minutes a day significantly reduced depression and loneliness.

AI thrives on the attention economy, but in the process, it's feeding anxiety, depression, and poor self-worth, especially among teens and young adults.

2. AI-Induced Sedentary Lifestyle

AI automates everything -- shopping, navigation, customer service, and even workouts. While convenient, this leads to a drastically reduced need for physical movement. The more AI takes over, the less active we become.

This sedentary behaviour is directly linked to:

* Obesity

* Cardiovascular diseases

* Type 2 diabetes

* Chronic back pain

...

The paradox? AI tools can recommend workouts or healthy diets, but they're also enabling a lifestyle that discourages physical exertion.

3. Blue Light & Sleep Disruption from AI-Driven Devices

Smartphones, tablets, and smart assistants are all AI-integrated. Using them late at night -- especially for AI-curated videos or chats -- leads to overstimulation and delayed sleep onset.

The blue light emitted suppresses melatonin production, disrupting circadian rhythms and increasing the risk of insomnia and fatigue. Over time, this can lead to serious health issues like:

* Hypertension

* Mood disorders

* Impaired cognitive function

...

4. AI Errors in Healthcare

AI in diagnostics and health predictions has shown promise. But AI is not immune to bias or error. If trained on incomplete or skewed data, AI tools can misdiagnose, miss warning signs, or suggest inappropriate treatments.

In 2019, a major health algorithm in the U.S. was found to be racially biased -- prioritising white patients over Black patients for care management programs.

When healthcare decisions rely heavily on flawed AI models, the result can be delayed treatment, worsened conditions, or even fatalities.

5. Job Anxiety and Economic Stress

AI is replacing jobs, especially in customer support, logistics, and manufacturing. The fear of redundancy, the pressure to upskill, and the unpredictability of employment are taking a serious mental toll on workers worldwide.

Burnout, insomnia, anxiety, and even suicidal thoughts are becoming common in workplaces undergoing digital transformation.

AI isn't just changing jobs; it's changing how people feel about their own relevance.

With a construction scene revolving around major institutional, hospitality and public and technology investments that is described as "steady" by John Hinshaw, president of Calhoun Construction, he also notes that the use of artificial intelligence is generating considerable curiosity within the construction industry in Louisville.

Proposal development, marketing, specification review, meeting minutes and document search are current uses. However, he says relatively few firms are openly sharing the full extent of their AI implementation.

"The opportunity is significant, but responsible use requires clear guardrails," Hinshaw says. "Firms need processes for protecting confidential information, verifying AI-generated content and maintaining human accountability. Used correctly, AI can help teams work more efficiently without replacing the judgment and experience required to deliver construction projects.

"We don't see AI replacing jobs -- we see it as a tool to help those that know how to use it to do their jobs more effectively and efficiently."

He says owners are using AI more during preconstruction.

"Contractors are investing additional effort in cost modeling, phasing, site logistics, procurement planning and stakeholder communication before construction begins," he says. "The teams that distinguish themselves are often those that give the owner confidence that the project is already organized and under control."

While AI continues to be a topic of discussion, Hinshaw says Louisville is seeing developments in various areas including its roadways. The Interstate 65 Corridor Project is a five-mile section on which three aging bridges -- the Kentucky Street/Brook Street bridge; Hill Street/CSX Railroad/Burnett Avenue bridge; and Bradley Avenue bridge -- are being replaced.

Another closely watched development is the planned conversion of the former 27-story Humana headquarters into a 1,000-room convention-style hotel. Plans for the 525,000-sq-ft building, considered a Louisville landmark, include multiple ballrooms, more than 100,000 sq ft of meeting space and multiple food and beverage concepts.

"The project could strengthen Louisville's ability to compete for larger conventions and national events," Hinshaw says.

Data center development continues to accelerate. Meta's $800-million data center in Jeffersonville is expected to become operational in 2026, while a hyperscale campus is proposed on approximately 150 acres along Camp Ground Road.

"We expect data centers to remain an important part of the regional construction market. The media seems to be announcing new ones pretty much weekly," Hinshaw says.

These facilities create substantial labor demand, particularly for electrical, which places pressure on an already constrained skilled-labor market.

"Electricians, line workers and other power-sector specialists are in especially high demand," he says.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can give busy people something that they lack and need: More time. That concept is one of the core ideas behind a conference planned for October in Hershey and sponsored by Goodwill Keystone.

Open to all nonprofit organizations, the Goodwill AI Networking Summit (GAINS) is intended to show attendees how to improve their operations and to better assist their clients by harnessing the power of AI.

"This new technology is transformational for nonprofits," said Ed Lada Jr., president and CEO of Goodwill Keystone that operates in 22 counties throughout Central Pennsylvania and the Lehigh Valley. "It allows us to serve more people in more profound ways, while also being good stewards of our resources."

He added that his organization is the first Goodwill in the country to provide AI literacy as part of its workforce and employee development programs.

Last December, the organization held its first GAINS, and more than 300 leaders of Goodwills nationwide attended.

This year, the summit has been opened to other nonprofits that will learn how AI software can support their missions, as well as workforce development and support services, finance and accounting duties, and other processes.

"We found last year's summit to be such a profound resource that we wanted every Pennsylvania nonprofit to have the opportunity to benefit from it, as well," Lada said.

More about the summit

Depending on how many organizations register, the first two days of the summit will be geared toward people and public officials who work in operations, human resources, technology, fundraising communications, programs, or organizational strategy.

"We've heard a lot of interest from nonprofits and public officials, but we need them to hit that register button, so we can be sure to provide the right sessions," Lada said.

However, if there aren't enough nonprofit registrations, portions of the summit geared to nonprofits might be cut to one day, he said.

With that caveat in mind, the schedule would include the following.

* Monday, Oct. 12 would be focused on challenges common across Pennsylvania nonprofits, with opportunities to engage with leaders from the nonprofit, workforce, government and technology sectors.

* On Tuesday, Oct. 13, attendees would work alongside experts who are developing AI tools, including OpenAI, Microsoft, and Anthropic.

Speakers and sponsors will include a mix of Goodwill and industry leaders, as well as AI companies, Lada said. He noted that additional training on Oct. 14-15 is currently set aside only for Goodwill organizations, and more than 200 Goodwills nationwide have registered for GAINS so far.

Putting ideas into action

Tripp Harrison, Goodwill Northern New England president and CEO, said he and several of his coworkers attended last year, and about 15 people from his staff will be going this year.

The business owners who navigate complexity well share one habit: they delay certainty long enough to understand what they're actually dealing with. Here's how to do that in practice.

You already know how to make better decisions in business. The problem is the world your decision-making tools were built for doesn't exist anymore.

Nobody sent a memo. There was no moment where someone announced that economics, banking, technology, and marketing had all crossed a complexity threshold that made pattern-matching from experience unreliable. The concepts accumulated. "Interest rates." "AI." "The algorithm." "Inflation." "Going viral." Each one sounds like a single thing. None of them are. And the gap between what those words seem to mean and what they actually describe is where a lot of business decisions quietly go wrong.

The last time most of us practiced this skill

Think back to the last time you were required to analyze something slowly. To read a text carefully and ask: what does this mean, what is the author assuming, what is the evidence, and what am I being asked to conclude?

For most people, the answer is high school or college: literature class, maybe a philosophy course. Somewhere in there, someone asked you to think beneath the surface of a text before you decided what it meant.

Then you entered the working world, and the reward structure flipped. Speed was valued over depth. Decisiveness beat deliberation. "Trust your gut" became professional advice. And for a long time, in a relatively stable environment where your experience was a good predictor of outcomes, that worked.

The problem is the environment changed. The concepts that now determine whether your business grows or contracts (pricing dynamics, search visibility, consumer psychology, credit conditions) became genuinely complex. They stopped behaving the way intuition predicts. The thinking tools most of us carry, built for speed and pattern-matching, haven't kept up.

The world is mostly gray and we keep wishing it were simple

Here's a phrase you've heard: "The economy is strong."

Underneath that phrase: there is no single economy. There's the stock market economy (asset prices), the labor economy (employment and wages), the consumer economy (spending and debt loads), the small business economy (revenue, margins, access to credit), and the real estate economy (values and rents). These move in different directions simultaneously. In 2022 and 2023, the stock market dropped 20%, unemployment sat at historic lows, small business failure rates rose, and real estate prices climbed in some markets while falling in others -- all at the same time.

"The economy is strong" describes one of those markets. It may describe none of yours.

A business owner making marketing decisions based on "the economy is strong" may be serving customers whose consumer debt load makes them spend less on exactly what you sell, in a region where commercial rents are rising faster than revenue. The headl
title: How to Make Better Decisions in Business When Everything Changed
author: DIYMarketers

The SIET-SINDA Charity Golf 2026 is happening on 28 August 2026 at Sembawang Country Club, bringing golfers, donors, corporate partners, families, and education supporters together for a day of golf that's all about giving back.

The campaign aims to raise S$50,000 to support deserving Indian students who need financial help to continue their post-secondary education, giving them a little more support to keep going and work towards their goals.

Funds raised will support education assistance provided by the Singapore Indian Education Trust (SIET), including bursaries and interest-free education loans.

Helping Students Keep Going

SIET has been supporting Indian students since 1967, when Mr. Kandisami started the organization together with community and business leaders.

The organization was set up to support students who could not afford the education they deserved. Its scholarships and loans help students stay on track with their studies and work towards their career goals.

Today, SIET supports more than 1,000 students each year through bursaries and interest-free loans. The support helps ease financial pressure on students and their families, giving students more breathing room to focus on their studies.

The charity golf campaign will help SIET keep this work going and reach even more students who need a helping hand.

For Students, The Support Can Mean A Lot

The impact of SIET's support can be seen through the experiences shared by students and donors.

One donor shared that their family has sponsored 12 nursing scholarships each year for the past three years, with each scholarship worth S$1,000. The scholarships come without a bond and are meant to help students finish their studies without constantly stressing about their finances.

The donor also shared that seeing how donations can support families in need encouraged their family to give back through education.

For students receiving the support, the financial assistance can take some weight off their shoulders.

One student pursuing biomedical science said SIET provided an interest-free student education loan, allowing them to focus on their studies and family without having to worry as much about money.

Another student receiving financial assistance said it helped ease the financial pressure on their mother.

A former beneficiary also shared how SIET's support helped shape their education and career, showing how a little financial help at the right time can go a long way. After completing an honors degree in engineering, the beneficiary went on to become a flight engineer with Singapore Technologies Aerospace before working with the Defence Science and Technology Agency.

Another beneficiary said SIET gave them the opportunity to pursue their medical ambitions.

Creating More Opportunities

Financial assistance is one part of the support students can receive.

One beneficiary also highlighted how corporate partners could offer internships and learning opportunities, giving student
title: Support SIET-SINDA Charity Golf 2026 And Help Indian Students Facing Financial Hardship
author: Wake Up Singapore

content:
An Uzbek student living in Singapore has shown viewers his apartment setup, including his bedroom, study area, and the greenery outside his window.

The student shared the video as "day one" of living alone in Singapore and said he lives in Bukit Gombak, which he described as a convenient location because it is not far from his university.

A Small Space In Bukit Gombak

In the video, the student showed the building where he lives, saying it has 12 floors and that his unit is on the eighth floor.

Inside, he showed his personal space, including his bed, study and work area, shelf, books, MacBook, and other belongings.

He said the space was not very large but that he had managed to fit what he needed. The room also has air conditioning and two fans, which he said were useful because Singapore is hot.

The student said he wanted to make the space feel more personal and asked viewers for decoration ideas.

One feature he particularly liked was the view from his window. He showed greenery surrounding the area and said he did not expect to wake up to so much greenery when he first moved to Singapore.

He also pointed out that the MRT passes through the area. According to the student, he enjoys watching the trains go past from his window.

Viewers Question The Rental Arrangement

The discussion became more focused on the rental cost after the student revealed that the accommodation costs S$1,500 in total.

He explained that three students would share the accommodation, bringing the cost to S$500 per person.

Some viewers initially got the wrong idea from the video and thought S$1,500 was being paid for one shared room. Others questioned whether S$500 per person was actually expensive when three people were splitting the room.

One commenter said S$500 per person was pretty reasonable, especially since the accommodation was near an MRT station. Another said shared rooms in Singapore can commonly go for around S$400 per person.

Others compared the price with different rental options, pointing out that costs can vary quite a bit depending on the location, availability, and type of accommodation.

The student later clarified in the comments that he was renting the room rather than the entire apartment. He also said that he was from Uzbekistan.

Another commenter, who identified themselves as working in real estate, said the arrangement was not necessarily a scam and pointed to Singapore's high rental costs.

Questions Over Privacy and Shared Facilities

The video also prompted viewers to question whether showing the location of his home online could create privacy or safety concerns.

Some commenters asked why he was showing where he lived, while others said that the information shown in the video was not necessarily enough to create a serious problem.

There were also questions about access to the rest of the apartment, including the toilet, living room, and kitchen.

One commenter said access to shared areas could depend on the homeowner and rental arr
title: Uzbek Student Shows His SG Apartment, Viewers Debate If S$500 Shared-Room Rent Is Too Much
author: Wake Up Singapore

content:
A recent preview of the RTS Link has given Singaporeans a closer look at the train station and the facilities available for passengers travelling between Singapore and Johor Bahru.

The commuter highlighted the large number of counters, spacious walkways, travelators and luggage-scanning facilities at the station. The preview also showed safety barriers, a ticket booth and what was described as a large counter area for passengers.

The station is connected to JB Central, with the creator saying passengers can reach the Malaysian station within about five minutes by train. The preview also focused on the amount of walking involved inside the station while noting that travelators are available to make parts of the journey easier.

A Closer Look At The Station

The preview showed several features designed for passengers moving through the station. These included luggage scanners, multiple walkways and travelators, plus plenty of open space for passengers to get around without feeling too cramped.

The creator also checked out the station's toilets, saying they looked more like something you'd find in a five-star hotel. Naturally, commenters had questions about whether they'd stay this clean once the crowds start rolling in, with some wondering how well the facilities would be maintained long term.

The RTS app also got a mention during the preview. The creator encouraged viewers to download it, saying it could make the whole travel and payment process a lot more convenient.

Ticket Prices Remain A Major Question

One of the biggest discussion points among commenters was the eventual ticket price.

The creator jokingly wondered whether a ticket could cost around S$5 each way. Other commenters questioned whether that would be realistic, with some suggesting that a higher fare could make regular trips expensive.

One commenter calculated that a S$30 round trip, if taken for 20 working days, could add up to around S$600 a month. Another commenter pointed out that the ticket price would be an important factor in deciding whether to use the train regularly.

The preview itself does not provide a confirmed RTS Link ticket price. The discussion therefore remains focused on what passengers may eventually have to pay.

Walking And Immigration Clearance Draw Attention

While the train journey to JB Central was described as taking about five minutes, several commenters focused on the distance passengers may need to walk within the station.

Some said the walking distance could be significantly longer than at the existing Woodlands CIQ, while others joked about using the station as an opportunity to hit their daily step targets. The creator also noted that passengers entering the JB customs area may encounter more walking, with travelators covering part of the route.

Immigration clearance was another point raised in the comments. One commenter said clearance could take around 25 minutes, while the creator suggested that the process could be faster because passe
title: TikToker Gives Upcoming RTS Link Preview, Showing New Facilities And Routes To JB
author: Wake Up Singapore

content:
Technology is creeping into every facet of our lives, for better or for worse is in the eye of the beholder, but it is certainly here to stay.

Australians are grappling with the prospects of AI replacing jobs, privacy breaches, misinformation and digital exclusion, while also benefiting from technology designed to make everyday tasks easier.

We want to hear your stories and experiences in our live blog below, where you can also put your questions to cybersecurity expert Mihai Lazarescu from Curtin University and the ABC's AI reporter Cam Wilson.
title: How has AI and tech changed your life? Australians share their stories
author: Australian Broadcasting Corporation

content:
Indian CEOs must build real AI products and solutions, moving beyond simple chatbot experiments. Companies are accelerating AI adoption and need to identify complex problems for dedicated task forces. Anthropic India is collaborating with major banks and institutions on various AI initiatives. McKinsey estimates AI's economic value at $4.4 trillion, with India investing billions.

Indian CEOs need to move beyond experimenting with AI chatbots and start building real products and solutions with the technology, Anthropic India MD Irina Ghose said, as enterprises accelerate AI adoption.

"Use it for yourself to build things, not just ask questions," Ghose said during a panel discussion at The Economic Times World Leaders Forum in New Delhi, urging CEOs to identify their most complex business problem and create a dedicated task force to solve it using AI.

"If you put across the biggest out there, the rest will surely happen," she said.

Anthropic is already working with Indian enterprises and institutions across sectors. Ghose said the company is working with Axis Bank and Kotak Bank on engineering productivity, NPCI on agentic AI solutions, and systems integrators including TCS and Infosys.

It is also working with governments and NGOs on agriculture, education, skilling, healthcare and life sciences. Its AI for Science team is working with IISc on antivenom discovery, while it is working with Digital Green on AI-powered responses to farmers in multiple languages.

"Our mission here remains that it's not with a playbook that we've come in; it's to co-create the playbook which will work for India and then we take it globally," Ghose said.

AI opportunity could be worth $4.4 trillion

Ghose cited McKinsey research estimating the economic value of AI at $4.4 trillion.

Indian companies currently invest around $2.6-2.8 billion in AI, according to research cited during the discussion, with companies surveyed by McKinsey planning to significantly increase investment over the next two years.

McKinsey partner Cheryl Lim said, however, that investing in AI does not automatically translate into business value.

While 80-90% of companies say they are investing in AI, a similar proportion say they have yet to see significant value from those investments, she said.

"The bigger part is how do we help our talent prepare for it, and what's the change management in place," Lim said.

Companies that succeed will be those that redesign workflows, upskill and reskill employees and address anxiety around AI replacing jobs, she added.

India's local needs meet global AI ambitions

SAP President-Asia Pacific Verena Siow said SAP's three-decade presence in India has helped it understand local requirements while developing technology for global markets.

Its Bengaluru labs are the company's largest outside Germany, with around 40% of the innovation it deploys globally developed from India, she said.

Ghose said local data residency and inference capabilities could furthe
title: Indian CEOs encouraged to innovate by creating impactful AI products beyond simple chatbot experiments
author: ETCIO.com

content:
University of Sydney (USyd) staff are set to strike for 24 hours on Wednesday 2nd September. This protected industrial action received overwhelming support from members of the USyd branch of the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU). What does this mean for students?

Staff Working Conditions are Student Learning Conditions

Have you ever received a mark without feedback? Are you annoyed at pre-recorded lectures which feel like YouTube slop? Have you struggled to get a response from an overworked academic? Has your tutorial had the student-teacher ratio of an underfunded high school? Have you experienced confusing last-minute room changes?

These are all symptoms of an increasingly corporatised and strained university sector, where university executives care more about filling their pockets than student and staff working and learning conditions. The goals of management are in direct opposition to the needs of students, and the strike is a chance for both staff and students to win a better university.

Every four years, staff and university management re-negotiate their enterprise agreement, which governs staff pay and working conditions. The last round of negotiations lasted almost two years, making it the longest running period of industrial action at an Australian university, with nine full days of non-consecutive strikes.

The union's log of claims details the issues central to the dispute between management and USyd staff. Included in this log of claims is a flat 20 per cent salary increase for all staff over the course of the agreement, protections for non-permanent full time employees, and protections for freedom of expression on campus. There has been a continued emphasis throughout Union activity that staff working conditions are student learning conditions. What do the strikers want to achieve? How will this improve your education and how can you help?

The Importance of Students on the Picket Line

The NTEU's picket line protocols somewhat constrain how union members are formally allowed to conduct themselves on strike. According to the protocols, when a "staff member, student or visitor indicates that she or he still intends to enter the University, the picketers will allow the person to pass without further disruption".

The upcoming strike follows a failed stop work action on August 10 that did not go ahead due to an administrative error from Branch President Peter Chen. Unlike a strike, stop work actions do not include picket lines. A picket line is a militant tool for unionists to oppose scabbing workers who seek to undermine these strikes. The NTEU's counter-intuitive picketline protocols make it especially important for students to be at the forefront of the picket line, as they are not inhibited by the restrictions invented by Union bureaucrats.

During the 2021-23 strike period, students organised a variety of militant actions. These included publicising the strikes in class, Zoom-bombing scab tutorials, mobilising contingen
title: 'Which Side Are You On?': How You Can Help Striking Staff
author: honisoit.com

content: Artificial intelligence has created a difficult question for companies and employees alike: if machines can perform more tasks, what happens to human jobs? Ravi Kumar S, the Indian-origin CEO of Cognizant, has spent much of his recent career examining that question from inside one of the world's largest technology services companies.Kumar has been named to TIME100 AI 2026 for the second consecutive year. His influence comes not from building a frontier chatbot, but from thinking about how AI will change organisations, workers and the way companies operate. Cognizant announced the recognition on August 27, highlighting Kumar's work on enterprise AI and workforce transformation.A scientist before becoming a technology CEOKumar's background is unusual for a technology executive. He trained as a nuclear scientist before moving into the technology and consulting industry.At Cognizant, he now leads a global organisation with hundreds of thousands of employees and thousands of AI engagements across industries.His focus is increasingly on what happens when AI moves from experimental projects into everyday business operations.Will AI replace jobs?Kumar's view is more complicated than a simple prediction that AI will either destroy or create jobs.He argues that many jobs are likely to remain, but the tasks within those jobs will change. As AI takes over repetitive or routine activities, employees could spend more time on work requiring judgement, creativity, collaboration and domain expertise.That shift has implications for students entering the workforce.A degree may get a candidate into an organisation, but the ability to work alongside AI could increasingly determine how valuable that employee becomes.From AI tools to AI-powered organisationsCognizant's AI strategy includes what it describes as enterprise agentification -- using AI agents to perform and coordinate tasks within business processes.Kumar has also promoted context engineering, an approach aimed at giving AI systems access to the information, workflows and decision-making context needed to perform useful work inside an organisation.The company's 2026 announcement said it has expanded AI deployments across industries while developing approaches around hyperproductivity, industrialised AI and enterprise agentification.What students should watchFor students and young professionals, Kumar's TIME100 AI recognition highlights an important change in the technology job market.AI may not simply create a new category of "AI jobs". It could change existing jobs across finance, healthcare, manufacturing, consulting, software and other sectors.That means learning AI tools may become as important as learning the underlying professional discipline.Cognizant has also invested in AI training for its workforce. title: 2026 TIME100 AI: From nuclear science to Cognizant CEO, how Ravi Kumar S is preparing workers for the AI era

content:
TCS just rolled out something called TCS ADD AgentHub, aimed at helping drug makers actually put AI to use in their day-to-day work. Basically, it hands off a lot of the repetitive stuff in clinical trials -- sifting through research papers, crunching data, keeping workflows moving -- to AI agents instead of people. But TCS is quick to point out humans aren't getting cut out of the loop entirely; people still call the shots and oversee what the AI's doing.

Basically, TCS ADD AgentHub lets pharma companies plug specialised AI agents into their R&D work. TCS points out it was built for pharma, since it's such a heavily regulated space, where firms have to weigh what AI can do against strict rules around safety, oversight, and audits.

"TCS ADD AgentHub is a reliable, enterprise-grade, role-based AI platform that will enable our clients to accelerate drug development through the use of agent-based AI at scale," says Debashis Ghosh, President of the Life Sciences and Healthcare division at TCS. "It facilitates the transition from reactive operations to proactive, scalable, and audit-ready processes within an ever-changing regulatory environment."

How does TCS ADD AgentHub work?

Instead of assigning all tasks to a single AI system, TCS ADD AgentHub allows pharmaceutical companies to use different AI agents for distinct functions. According to the company, these agents can assist with tasks related to clinical development and pharmacovigilance (the process of monitoring drug safety after development or market launch).

For example, AI agents can help with data entry, coding, information review, and medical literature analysis. They can also assist in study design, converting clinical trial protocols into digital formats, reviewing clinical data, and supporting medical oversight. TCS notes that companies can adopt these AI agents gradually, depending on their specific needs and existing technology.

TCS states that its AI platform could also reduce some of the repetitive work associated with drug development. Solutions based on this platform have demonstrated efficiency gains of up to 40% in clinical data management, while metadata-driven automation can cut the effort required to set up clinical studies by up to 30%. The company also claims cost savings of up to 30% in end-to-end safety case processing, while AI-based safety agents can reduce the workload associated with quality control by up to 50%.

Will AI replace jobs in drug development?

So, does this mean AI now threatens jobs in drug development? Not exactly -- at least according to TCS. The company maintains that the goal is not to replace scientists or exclude humans from the process. Instead, its "human-AI operating model" integrates AI agents alongside people, keeping humans responsible for governance and key decision-making.

The new AI agent platform from TCS is going to be really helpful for companies. This TCS platform will let these companies give all the time-consuming tasks to the
title: TCS Uses AI to Speed Up Drug Discovery and Clinical Trials
author: The Hans India

content:
There doesn't seem to be much pain in Rebekah Brown land. The head of the Australian National University offered a positive view of the future but no mention of any bumpy road getting there.

As she faced the press, Professor Brown, the ANU's interim vice-chancellor, exuded warm words about the future of the "fantastic institution" she now leads - but no details of any pain the recovery from a series of crises might involve.

The only leader of the ANU left standing after both the previous vice-chancellor and chancellor resigned faced the press to talk about the newly-published "ANU by 2030" strategy.

The tough questions bounced at her: How much would she need to take out of the salary bill? Would she be in the running to take over the job permanently? How many jobs would go when AI took over administrative work? When will the ANU's deficit be cleared?

But hard questions didn't get hard answers. She showed all the skill of a dead-bat cricketer determined to get back to the pavilion with her wicket still standing.

"When do you think your deficit will have gone? When will the negative become positive?" she was asked.

"We, of course, hope that's sooner rather than later. There's a lot of structural forces globally that we're planning and working through. But I really would prefer ... Today is a day for our community. It's a day for us to celebrate," she replied, alluding to the 80 birthday of the ANU and the reopening of University House, six years after it was damaged by hail.

It's true that University House is a magnificent mid-century-modern accommodation place - a hotel in all but name - for senior people, complete with Boffins Restaurant and Private Dining Room "offering refined dining in a heritage setting".

But the questions at the press conference concentrated, unhelpfully perhaps, on how the ANU would achieve the sunny uplands outlined in the glossy "ANU by 2030" brochure which Professor Brown was also there to talk about.

"Will that implementation plan include guarantees about staff numbers," a reporter asked. Would the way the ANU was governed be improved?

"Well, our community's been really clear," was the response, "and so is our council about the really important role that our staff, students, and alumni play in our governance. We talk in the strategy around meaningful participation in university and institutional decision-making, and I expect that we will see that throughout all our internal governance structures."

The "ANU by 2030" document says: "Artificial intelligence enabled services will handle the routine reliably and at scale, freeing our people for the wisdom and care that only people can provide. It imagines that "human and machine intelligence work in concert, expanding what we can imagine, discover and achieve together".

So, reporters sought detail from Professor Brown. Would AI replace jobs?

On this, she seemed to be clearish: "No. We're, we're really, really clear that ... We're already using AI at ANU, like un
title: No pain in Rebekah Brown land as the ANU wrestles with its deep problems
author: Bega District News

content:
From marketing homes to building them smarter, AI is moving into the core of India's real estate business.

In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) in India's real estate sector was largely confined to the customer-facing side of the business. Virtual property tours, chatbots answering buyer queries, personalised recommendations and smarter digital marketing were among the first applications developers experimented with.

That was the easy part.

Now, a much bigger shift is happening behind construction barricades, inside project offices and across boardrooms where developers are increasingly relying on AI to decide what to build, when to build it, how much it will cost and whether a project is likely to run into trouble long before delays begin to show up on site.

The conversations around AI inside real estate companies have changed remarkably over the past year.

Also Read: GenAI can add $14-17 billion to India's real estate economy: Report

The opportunity is massive. India's real estate sector is currently valued at $650 billion, projected to become a $5.8-trillion industry by 2047, according to the India Brand Equity Foundation (IBEF). But to get there, developers will have to build more, build faster and build smarter. Increasingly, they believe AI can help do all three. A joint EY-Parthenon and CREDAI report estimates GenAI alone could add $14-17 billion to the sector's Gross Value Added over the next seven years by improving productivity, shortening project timelines and boosting sales.

"About 18 months ago, developers were asking us, 'What can AI do?' Today, the question is, 'How quickly can we roll this out on our next project?'," Iesh Dixit, co-founder and CEO of construction management platform Powerplay, told ET Online.

That shift reflects a broader change across the industry.

According to the EY-Parthenon-CREDAI report, developers adopting GenAI could see 30-50% higher sales velocity, around 30% faster product launches, 20-50% gains in workforce productivity and 20-50% lower customer acquisition costs, driven by AI-powered customer intelligence, automated design workflows and predictive project monitoring.

"GenAI is fast becoming central to value creation and competitiveness, making inaction a growing strategic risk," said Chaitanya Seth, Partner, Real Estate at EY-Parthenon India. "This is not about incremental digitisation. It is about rewiring the operating model."

The underlying reason is simple. Real estate has always been a business built on fragmented information.

Every project generates thousands of drawings, contracts, approvals, site photographs, procurement records, spreadsheets, WhatsApp messages and progress reports. Traditionally, making sense of all this depended heavily on experience and manual coordination.

AI changes that equation.

Unlike older enterprise software that required structured databases and extensive employee training, today's AI models can understand engineering drawings, site images, vo
title: Cement, bricks and AI: India's $650-billion real estate industry has a new formula
author: Economic Times
